title: Children in the sun: a practical protection plan for families
intro: Outdoor play is valuable, and sun protection can be part of the plan before a child gets uncomfortable. Ultraviolet radiation can damage skin and eyes even when the weather does not feel very hot. Childhood sunburn adds to later skin-cancer risk. Combine shade, clothing and suitable sunscreen, while also preventing overheating. No single measure blocks all exposure, and children with darker skin still need protection.

sections.heading: Plan around ultraviolet exposure, not just temperature
paragraphs: Check the local UV forecast and arrange longer outdoor activities for times with less intense sun where possible. Clouds and a cool breeze do not reliably remove UV exposure. Water, sand and other surfaces can reflect it. Choose a shaded place for breaks and check where the shade moves during the day. A parasol is useful but does not replace clothing and protection for exposed skin. Ask a pharmacist or clinician if a child's medicine or skin condition increases sun sensitivity.

sections.heading: Clothing and shade make protection easier
paragraphs: Choose comfortable clothing that covers the shoulders and other exposed areas, a hat protecting the face, ears and neck, and well-fitting UV-protective sunglasses. Avoid making the child too hot with unnecessary layers. For swimming, suitable sun-protective clothing helps but exposed areas still need attention. Keep young babies out of direct sunlight, especially those under six months. Use an appropriate ventilated pram shade rather than covering a pushchair with a blanket, which can trap heat. Check the baby regularly.

sections.heading: Use sunscreen generously and repeatedly
paragraphs: For children old enough for sunscreen, choose a broad-spectrum product protecting against UVA and UVB, with SPF of at least 30, and follow its instructions. Cover exposed areas thoroughly, including commonly missed ears, neck and tops of feet. Reapply at least every two hours and promptly after swimming, sweating or towel drying, even with a water-resistant product. Ask for specific advice for a baby under six months rather than relying on sunscreen. A higher SPF does not mean unlimited time outside or remove the need to reapply.

sections.heading: Make an ordinary routine that adults can maintain
paragraphs: Keep hats, sunscreen and appropriate drinks with the items you pack for outings. Agree who checks protection when a child moves between home, school, sports and another caregiver. Offer manageable choices, such as which suitable hat to wear, while the adult remains responsible for adequate protection. Explain the plan in simple language and model it yourself. Remember that shade and cool clothing also help with heat, while sunscreen does not prevent dehydration or heatstroke. Babies' feeding and fluid needs require age-appropriate advice; do not dilute formula to make extra drinks.

sections.heading: Respond early to sunburn or overheating
paragraphs: Move a sunburned child out of the sun, cool the skin gently without ice and do not break blisters. Avoid making a baby too cold. Get prompt medical advice for sunburn in a baby or young child, blistering or swollen skin, dehydration, fever or marked illness. Confusion, collapse, a seizure or suspected heatstroke needs emergency help and cooling while help arrives. Do not force drinks into a drowsy or unconscious child. Skin redness can be less obvious on darker skin, so also notice tenderness and heat.

examples.title: An outdoor lesson — hypothetical example
examples.text: A caregiver checks the forecast before a long outdoor lesson, packs a hat and sunscreen and asks who will supervise reapplication. They arrange a shaded break rather than assuming the morning application protects the whole day.

examples.title: A hot walk with a baby — hypothetical example
examples.text: A family chooses a cooler time, uses a ventilated sunshade and checks the baby frequently. They do not drape a blanket over the pram. If the baby seems unwell or develops sunburn, they seek medical advice rather than simply adding sunscreen.

questions: What protection suits my child's age, skin condition and medicines?
Who will maintain shade, clothing and sunscreen during school, sport or childcare?
Which signs of sunburn, dehydration or heat illness require medical help?
